      <h1 class="talk-title">A Gentle Introduction to Targets</h1>
    </header>

    <!-- Body Section -->
    <div class="talk-body">

      <!-- Main Description -->
      <section class="talk-description">
        <p>Data analysis is an iterative process. Data cleaning, exploratory data analysis (EDA), and model fitting are rarely run without a hitch from start to finish. Each step takes time, and often requires revisiting earlier steps to correct for newly discovered problems. For example, in performing EDA, you can unearth a text issue that requires revisiting data cleaning. When you are finally done with the analysis, you will need to reproduce it to check it all works as expected.</p>
<p>To reproduce the analysis, there is a temptation to run the code again from the top, which may take a long time. You can save time by saving model outputs, but if you make a change to an earlier data cleaning step, you’ll need to update everything that depends on that. You can write code to manage these dependencies, but this is a hard problem. Fortunately, &quot;pipeline tools&quot; are an existing approach to manage these dependencies. They take care of the details of watching which files and relevant code changes, and only run the necessary parts. The {targets} R package is one popular pipeline approach, providing extensive documentation and user support. However, it presents a different coding practice that might not be familiar.</p>
<p>In this interactive workshop, I will gently introduce the ideas behind {targets}, and will live code a data analysis using {targets} from scratch, warts and all. I encourage questions throughout the live coding workshop, so you can understand the process and see how this could benefit your own work.</p>
<p>I have three goals in this workshop:</p>
<ol>
<li>To convince you {targets} is worth learning, and that you can use it</li>
<li>For you to be able to start using {targets} after 45 minutes</li>
<li>For you to feel more confident writing functions</li>
</ol>

            <p>Dr. Nicholas (Nick) Tierney is a statistician, <a href="https://researchsoftware.org/">Research Software Engineer</a>, and freelance consultant with a PhD in Statistics who specializes in data analytics, R package development, and teaching.
